title: Friends, women, books
hookLine: three kinds of company, and books the most constant (Essays 3.3)

cards: Who do you actually spend your hours with? Not who you'd list on a form: who's really there, day after day, when you look back over a week? Montaigne asks himself that in the next essay of book three.
The French title calls it three kinds of commerce, meaning three kinds of dealings, three kinds of company. He names them without fuss: friends, women and books.
Then he weighs each one honestly: what it gives, and what it costs.

teach.h: FRIENDS: RARE, A GIFT OF CHANCE.
teach.b: First, friends. Montaigne prizes real friendship, where two minds talk freely and sharpen each other. But it's rare, he admits, and depends on finding the right person, and on that person staying.
A gift of chance. Second, the company of women. Here he writes frankly, as a man of his time, about love and attraction between men and women.
It is sweet, he says, it stirs the body and the feelings, but it is restless and can unsettle the mind. Readers today notice how his era frames it.
What he's weighing is closeness that is lovely and never fully in his control. Third, books. This, he says, is the steadiest company.

teach.h: BOOKS: THERE WHEN YOU WANT THEM.
teach.b: Books are there when he wants them and wait quietly when he doesn't; they don't sulk if he ignores them. They console him in solitude and help him pass dull hours.
They live in his library in the tower, where he walks while he thinks, because his thoughts fall asleep, he says, if he makes them sit. Fourth, the catch.

teach.h: EVEN BOOKS LEAVE THE BODY IDLE.
teach.b: Even books have a fault: they exercise the mind and leave the body idle. So no single company is enough.
A friend who talks back. A closeness that warms you, whatever shape it has in your life. Something steady on the shelf.
Each feeds what the others can't.

how: Readers of Montaigne's essay on three kinds of company often take it as a quiet inventory: friends, love, and books, each weighed for what it gives and what it costs.

o: the readers Montaigne wrote his book to please
Montaigne's first company: rare, a gift of chance
anyone who agrees with you about everything

games.q: three kinds of company: tap the pairs.

s: Montaigne says books are the steadiest of the three companies
they are there when he wants them and wait quietly when he doesn't.
he says his thoughts work best when he sits still
he says his thoughts fall asleep if he makes them sit; he walks while he thinks.
he says books have no faults at all
they exercise the mind and leave the body idle.

games.q: you're Montaigne in your tower library, thinking. what do you do with your body?
o: lie down with a book on your face.
games.why: he says his thoughts fall asleep if he makes them sit; so he walks.

practice: Bring to mind a friend who talks back to you honestly, and be glad they exist. Then someone close, whose warmth you feel, whatever that closeness looks like for you; then a book, a song or a page that has stayed with you.
Let each one sit with you for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Friends. The first of Montaigne's three companies: rare, a gift of chance, and worth weighing beside the other two. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: three companies. Friends by chance, love with its restlessness, books always on the shelf. Until tomorrow.
